pos: n. (outward show made to be seen; religious display performed for an audience)
etymology: Latin ostentatio, from ostendere, to show. The Sermon on the Mount treats it as the standing corruption of the three chief duties — alms, prayer and fasting.
biblical_def: Ostentation is religion performed for spectators. The Lord takes the three great duties in turn and attaches the same warning to each: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 6:1); “do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do… that they may have glory of men” (Mat 6:2); “they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men” (Mat 6:5). He names it as the governing principle of a whole party: “all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). The Pharisee's prayer is the specimen: “God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are” (Luk 18:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ostentation as outward show or appearance; ambitious display; vain show; a boastful display of anything, made to invite praise or flattery.
webster_full: OSTENTATION, n. Outward show or appearance.
2. Ambitious display; vain show; display of any thing dictated by vanity, or intended to invite praise or flattery.
Ostentation of endowments is a certain proof of the want of them.
OSTENTATIOUS, a. Making a display from vanity; boastful; fond of presenting one's endowments to others.
scriptures: Mat 6:1
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Mat 6:2

Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Mat 6:5

And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Mat 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
corruption_summary: The reward is thought to be forfeited by being seen, and the Lord locates the fault in the motive.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 6:1 has to be read alongside Matthew 5:16, where the same Preacher says let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven. The two are not in tension because the distinction is not visibility but purpose. Chapter 5 has men seeing the works and glorifying God; chapter 6 has men seeing the works and glorifying the doer. Being observed is unavoidable in most of a Christian's obedience; performing for the observation is the sin, and only the man himself can usually tell which is happening.

The phrase the Lord repeats is the quiet horror of the passage: they have their reward. The word is a commercial one, used of a receipt for payment in full. The hypocrite wanted to be admired, and he was admired; the transaction closed at the moment the admiration was received, and nothing is owing from heaven because nothing further was ever sought. This is not God withholding a reward in anger. It is a man being given exactly what he asked for, which is the most frightening form the judgment can take.

The remedy in Matthew 6:3 is deliberately impossible to systematise: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. It is not a rule about secrecy — a strict rule would itself become a performance, and the ostentatiously anonymous giver is a recognisable type. It is a picture of a man whose giving is so unselfconscious that he is not keeping his own accounts. Luke 18:11 shows the alternative endpoint, and its detail is exact: the Pharisee prayed thus with himself. He had an audience of one, and it was not God.
roots_summary: Greek theaomai (G2300), to be seen, gazed at; misthos (G3408), reward, wages; apecho (G568), to have in full, receipt; hupokrites (G5273), an actor, hypocrite.
roots_lines: Greek pros to theathenai autois (G2300) — to be seen of them; Matthew 6:1, 23:5.
Greek apechousin ton misthon (G568, G3408) — they have their reward, receipted in full; Matthew 6:2, 6:5, 6:16.
Greek hupokrites (G5273) — an actor wearing a mask; Matthew 6:2, 6:5, 6:16, 23:13–29.
usage: “That they may have glory of men” — and they do.
“They have their reward” — a receipt for payment in full.
“Prayed thus with himself” — an audience of one, and not God.

pos: n. (rudeness compounded with contempt; insulting language or treatment)
etymology: Latin contumelia, from contumere, to swell with pride — the same root as contumacy. The insult proceeds from a swollen estimate of oneself.
biblical_def: Contumely is insult delivered with contempt, and the Passion is the Bible's fullest account of it. The soldiers “platted a crown of thorns… and bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews” (Mat 27:29). The Servant foresaw it: “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting” (Isa 50:6). The psalm records the manner: “All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head” (Psa 22:7). Peter records the response: “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again” (1Pe 2:23). And Hebrews makes it an argument against fainting: “consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself” (Heb 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contumely as rudeness compounded of haughtiness and contempt; contemptuousness; insolence; contemptuous language.
webster_full: CONTUMELY, n. Rudeness compounded of haughtiness and contempt; contemptuousness; insolence; contemptuous language; reproach.
The oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contumely.
CONTUMELIOUS, a. Haughtily reproachful; contemptuous; insolent; rude and sarcastic.
scriptures: And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
Isa 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
Psa 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
Heb 12:3
For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds.
corruption_summary: Insult is answered in kind and called standing up for the truth, and the Lord had the best possible case for answering and did not.
corruption_paragraphs: First Peter 2:23 is stated in a way that removes the usual escape. When He was reviled, He reviled not again; when He suffered, He threatened not — and Peter's point in context is that this is left us as an example, that we should follow His steps. The passage is addressed to servants under unjust masters, which is to say to people with no power and no recourse, and it does not tell them their treatment is acceptable. It tells them what He did with worse, and where He put the case.

The clause that makes the silence possible is the last one: but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously. This is not a counsel to feel nothing or to pretend the insult was fair. It is a transfer of jurisdiction. The reason a man must answer contumely in kind is that he believes no one else will ever set the record straight; remove that belief and the necessity goes with it. Everything hard in Christian meekness depends on the doctrine of a final judgment being actually believed rather than merely affirmed.

Hebrews 12:3 gives the pastoral use and its verb is the important one: consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. The remedy for the slow exhaustion that contempt produces is not a technique but an act of attention — deliberately reckoning up what He took, and from whom, and for whose sake. The chapter is written to people who had not yet resisted unto blood, and it is meant to put a proportion on their trouble without dismissing it.
roots_summary: Greek empaizo (G1702), to mock; loidoreo (G3058), to revile; antilogia (G485), contradiction, gainsaying; Hebrew laag (H3932), to deride, laugh to scorn.
roots_lines: Greek empaizo (G1702) — to mock, make sport of; Matthew 27:29–31, 20:19, Luke 22:63.
Greek loidoreo (G3058) — to revile; 1 Peter 2:23, John 9:28, Acts 23:4.
Greek antilogia (G485) — contradiction, hostile speech; Hebrews 12:3, 6:16, 7:7, Jude 1:11.
usage: “Hail, King of the Jews” — the knee bowed, in mockery.
“Reviled not again… but committed himself” — a transfer of jurisdiction.
“Consider him that endured such contradiction” — an act of attention.

pos: n. (kindness of disposition; goodness that inclines toward the undeserving)
etymology: Latin benignitas, from bene, well, and gignere, to beget — well-born, and so well-disposed. The AV's word is kindness or goodness; the older divines use benignity of God's disposition toward sinners.
biblical_def: Benignity is the goodness of a disposition, and Scripture makes it an attribute of God before it is a duty of man. It appeared in a Person: “after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:4–5). It has an aim: “despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” (Rom 2:4). It is fruit, not effort: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness” (Gal 5:22). And it is commanded with a measure attached: “be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you” (Eph 4:32); “put on… kindness” (Col 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines benignity as goodness of nature; kindness of disposition; graciousness; a favorable disposition, mild and gracious.
webster_full: BENIGNITY, n. Goodness of nature; kindness of disposition which disposes to charity and acts of good will; graciousness.
2. Actual goodness; beneficence.
3. Salubrity; wholesome quality; that which promotes health.
BENIGN, a. Kind; of a kind disposition; gracious; generous; liberal.
scriptures: Tit 3:4
But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared,
Rom 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
Gal 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Eph 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Col 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
corruption_summary: God's kindness is read as indulgence, and Romans 2:4 says it is aimed at repentance and can be despised.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 2:4 is the verse that keeps the doctrine from softening into permissiveness, and its two verbs are both surprising. God's goodness can be despised — treated as of no account — and it leadeth thee to repentance, which is where it was always headed. Kindness in Scripture is not indifference to sin; it is the patience that makes repentance possible by not ending the matter at once. To read the delay as approval is to mistake the reason for the delay, and Paul says the man who does so is treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath.

Titus 3:4 gives the shape of divine benignity and it is the whole gospel in a sentence: the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared. Not a disposition inferred from providence but one that entered history at a point and can be dated. And the next clause guards it from every scheme of merit — not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us. Benignity toward the deserving is only justice; the word means something because those it reaches had nothing to commend them.

Ephesians 4:32 supplies the measure for the human version and it is ruinous to self-congratulation: be ye kind one to another, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. The standard is not proportionality to the offence but the treatment one has already received, which means the man with most to be forgiven has least ground for withholding it — the exact argument of the parable of the unforgiving servant. Galatians 5:22 adds that this is fruit rather than achievement: it grows on a tree that has been made alive, and cannot be manufactured by a man determined to seem pleasant.
roots_summary: Greek chrestotes (G5544), kindness, goodness; philanthropia (G5363), love toward man; agathosune (G19), goodness; eusplagchnos (G2155), tenderhearted.
roots_lines: Greek chrestotes (G5544) — kindness; Titus 3:4, Romans 2:4, 11:22, Galatians 5:22, Colossians 3:12.
Greek philanthropia (G5363) — love toward man; Titus 3:4, Acts 28:2.
Greek chrestos (G5543) — kind, gracious, easy; Ephesians 4:32, Luke 6:35, Matthew 11:30.
usage: “The kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared” — it can be dated.
“The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance” — and can be despised.
“Even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you” — the measure.

etymology: Latin docilitas, from docere, to teach — the same root as doctrine and doctor. Docility is not weakness of mind; it is the condition of having one that can still be taught.
biblical_def: Docility is teachableness, and Scripture attaches the promise of guidance to it: “The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way” (Psa 25:9). It is the mark of wisdom rather than of ignorance: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning” (Pro 9:9). James makes it the posture in which the word is received: “receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21). The Bereans are commended for it: they “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11). And God names whom He regards: “him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word” (Isa 66:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines docility as teachableness; readiness to learn; aptness to be taught; and, in a more general sense, tractableness.
webster_full: DOCILITY, n. Teachableness; readiness to learn; aptness to be taught.
2. In a more general sense, tractableness; ready submission.
DOCILE, a. Teachable; easily instructed; ready to learn.
2. Tractable; easily managed.
scriptures: Psa 25:9
The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 66:2
For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the LORD: but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.
corruption_summary: Teachableness is confused with credulity, and the Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to see whether an apostle was right.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17:11 holds the two halves together in a single sentence and neither survives without the other. The Bereans received the word with all readiness of mind — that is the docility — and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so — that is the discrimination. They were not credulous, since they checked; they were not cynical, since they checked in order to believe. Luke calls them more noble than the Thessalonians for the combination. A man who believes whatever he is told has no teachableness, only an absence of resistance, and he will be carried off by the next confident voice.

Proverbs 9:9 states the counter-intuitive law of the whole subject: give instruction to a wise man and he will be yet wiser. Teachableness is not a stage one passes through on the way to competence; it is the permanent condition of anyone who continues to grow, which is why the same chapter's fool is defined by his imperviousness. The practical test is simple and uncomfortable: when was a man last corrected on something that mattered, and what did he do? The answer will place him on the right chapter of Proverbs more accurately than any account he gives of himself.

Isaiah 66:2 is the most remarkable of these verses because of who is speaking and what He is looking at. The heaven is His throne and the earth His footstool, and all those things His hand has made — and to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word. The trembling is not fear of God's anger but a settled regard for what He has said, which is the deepest form docility takes. James 1:21 gives it the domestic name: receive with meekness the engrafted word, and the previous clause says to lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness first, because a cluttered man cannot be taught.
roots_summary: Hebrew anav (H6035), meek, humble; chared (H2730), trembling, reverent; Greek prautes (G4240), meekness; prothumia (G4288), readiness of mind.
roots_lines: Hebrew anav (H6035) — meek, humble; Psalm 25:9, 37:11, 149:4, Numbers 12:3.
Greek prothumia (G4288) — readiness of mind, eagerness; Acts 17:11, 2 Corinthians 8:11–12, 9:2.
Greek prautes (G4240) — meekness; James 1:21, 3:13, Galatians 6:1, 1 Peter 3:15.
usage: “Received the word with all readiness of mind… and searched the scriptures daily” — both halves.
“Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” — the permanent condition.
“Trembleth at my word” — and the speaker's throne is heaven.

pos: adj. (inborn; native to the mind, not derived from instruction or experience)
etymology: Latin innatus, inborn, from in- and nasci, to be born. Calvin's term is the sensus divinitatis — a sense of deity implanted in every man, which no one has to be taught.
biblical_def: An innate knowledge is one a man is born with. Paul says the moral law is such: the Gentiles “shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another” (Rom 2:14–15). So is a knowledge of God: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them” (Rom 1:19). It is reinforced from without — “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psa 19:1) — and inward: “he hath set the world in their heart” (Ecc 3:11). Its purpose is stated at Athens: “that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us” (Act 17:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines innate as inborn; native; natural; and innate ideas as ideas or notions supposed by some philosophers to be stamped on the mind at its first existence.
webster_full: INNATE, a. Inborn; native; natural; as innate worth.
Innate ideas, are such as are supposed to be stamped on the mind, at the moment when it begins to exist, or when it receives its being; a supposition now generally discarded.
INNATELY, adv. Naturally.
INNATENESS, n. The quality of being innate.
scriptures: Rom 2:14
For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves:
Rom 1:19
Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.
Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Ecc 3:11
He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
corruption_summary: An innate sense of God is taken to be enough, and Paul introduces it in order to establish that men are without excuse.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's entry records a philosophical fashion — the supposition of innate ideas, now generally discarded — and the theological claim is not the one Locke was arguing against. Calvin's sensus divinitatis is not a set of propositions stamped on the newborn mind; it is an ineradicable awareness that there is Someone, which shows itself in the universality of worship, in the fear that visits a man in extremity, and in the labour required to keep denying it. Romans 1 describes exactly that labour: men who hold the truth in unrighteousness, suppressing what they cannot uninstall.

The crucial point is the use Paul makes of the doctrine, because it runs opposite to how it is usually deployed. He introduces the innate knowledge not to reassure anyone but to close a defence: so that they are without excuse. The moral sense in Romans 2 does the same work against the moralist, since a conscience that accuses proves he knew the standard he broke. Innate knowledge in Scripture is never presented as a sufficient religion; it is presented as the ground on which the charge is laid.

Ecclesiastes 3:11 gives the experiential side and its phrasing is haunting: He hath set the world — or eternity — in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end. There is a capacity for the infinite in a creature who cannot fill it, which explains a great deal about human restlessness. Acts 17:27 says what it is for: that they should seek the Lord, feeling after Him in the dark, and He is not far. That is the missionary's warrant. He is not bringing a foreign notion to a mind with no category for it, but a name to a longing that was already there.
roots_summary: Greek phaneros (G5318), manifest, evident; suneidesis (G4893), conscience, co-knowledge; psélaphao (G5584), to feel after, grope; Hebrew olam (H5769), eternity, the world.
roots_lines: Greek to gnoston tou theou phaneron (G1110, G5318) — that which may be known of God is manifest; Romans 1:19.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience; Romans 2:15, 9:1, 1 Corinthians 8:7, Hebrews 9:14.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — eternity, the age; Ecclesiastes 3:11, 3:14, 12:5.
usage: “Written in their hearts” — and the conscience accusing or excusing.
“So that they are without excuse” — what the doctrine is for.
“He hath set the world in their heart” — a capacity no creature can fill.

pos: adj. (childish; belonging to a boy, and unfitting in a man)
etymology: Latin puerilis, from puer, a boy. Scripture distinguishes sharply between the child a Christian must become and the child he must stop being — and uses the same word group for both.
biblical_def: Puerile means childish where manhood is due. Paul marks the transition: “When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things” (1Co 13:11). He divides the two senses in one verse: “Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” (1Co 14:20). Immaturity has a symptom: “that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). It has a diet: “every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe” (Heb 5:13). And the other kind of childlikeness is required: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 18:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines puerile as boyish; childish; trifling; as a puerile amusement; and puerility as childishness, that which is trifling.
webster_full: PUERILE, a. Boyish; childish; trifling; as a puerile amusement.
PUERILITY, n. Childishness; boyishness; the manners or actions of a boy.
2. That which is puerile or childish; that which is trifling.
PUERILELY, adv. Childishly.
scriptures: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Heb 5:13
For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
Mat 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The command to become as little children is used to excuse the condition Paul tells men to grow out of.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 14:20 is the verse that sorts the two and it does the work in one line: in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. Childlikeness is commanded in dependence, in trust, in the absence of grudges and calculation, in the readiness to be carried. Childishness is forbidden in judgment, doctrine, stability and self-government. A church that quotes Matthew 18:3 to justify a shallow grasp of Scripture has taken a command about the heart and applied it to the head, and Paul had a congregation doing exactly that, which is why he wrote the sentence.

Ephesians 4:14 names the practical cost, and the image is nautical: children, tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men. A congregation that has not been taught has no ballast, and it will move with whatever is currently persuasive — not because its members are foolish but because nothing in them resists. The remedy in the surrounding verses is not caution but growth: speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ. Stability is a by-product of maturity, not a discipline of its own.

Hebrews 5:13 adds the sharpest word for anyone content to stay where he is: every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness. The failure is not intellectual but moral, since the next verse says the faculties are exercised by use. A believer of long standing who still cannot handle a hard passage or bear a hard providence has not lacked opportunity; and 1 Corinthians 13:11 describes the alternative in the plainest terms available — when I became a man, I put away childish things. The putting away was something Paul did.
roots_summary: Greek nepios (G3516), an infant, one without speech; teleios (G5046), full-grown, mature; paidion (G3813), a little child; kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed by waves.
roots_lines: Greek nepios (G3516) — infant, babe; 1 Corinthians 13:11, 14:20, Ephesians 4:14, Hebrews 5:13.
Greek paidion (G3813) — little child; Matthew 18:2–5 — the kind a man must become.
Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — tossed by waves; Ephesians 4:14 only.
usage: “In malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” — the sorting verse.
“Tossed to and fro… with every wind of doctrine” — a congregation without ballast.
“I put away childish things” — and the putting away was his own act.

pos: n. (an assembly of ministers and elders sitting as a court; in Geneva, the body charged with discipline)
etymology: Latin consistorium, a place of standing together. Geneva's Consistory met weekly, was composed of pastors and lay elders, and had power to admonish and to exclude from the table — and no power of the sword.
biblical_def: A consistory is a standing court of the church. Its warrant is the assembly at Jerusalem: “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6), concluding, “it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28). Discipline is committed to the gathered congregation: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17), and exercised “when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1Co 5:4). Its procedure protects the accused: “Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses” (1Ti 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines consistory as a place of justice in the spiritual court; the court of every diocesan bishop; and, in the Reformed churches, an assembly of ministers and elders for regulating ecclesiastical affairs.
webster_full: CONSISTORY, n. Primarily, a place of standing or meeting; an assembly.
2. A place of justice in the spiritual court, or the court itself.
3. An assembly of prelates; the college of cardinals at Rome.
4. In the Reformed churches, an assembly or council of ministers and elders.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ,
Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.
corruption_summary: A church court either becomes a tribunal answerable to nobody, or is quietly abolished and discipline with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures face each other and most congregations have seen one of them. The first is the court that forgets its limits: Geneva's Consistory could admonish and exclude from the table, and it could not fine, imprison or execute — those belonged to the magistrate, and the confusion of the two is exactly what made the Servetus case a stain. A church court's whole armoury is spiritual, and when it reaches for anything else it has stopped being a church court. The second failure is more common now: discipline abandoned entirely, so that a congregation has no way to address sin except gossip and departure, which are the two methods Scripture forbids.

Acts 15 is the model and its features are worth listing because they are so often absent. There was a real dispute; the apostles and elders came together specifically to consider it; both sides were heard at length, with much disputing; Scripture was consulted, not merely experience; a decision was reached and written down; and it was communicated to the churches affected with reasons attached. The formula in verse 28 — it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us — is the most careful sentence in the chapter, claiming the Spirit's guidance without claiming inspiration for the men.

First Timothy 5:19 is the procedural protection and the church ignores it constantly. Against an elder receive not an accusation but before two or three witnesses — receive not, which means the charge is not even entertained until the standard is met. This is not a shield for the powerful; it is a rule made necessary precisely because men in office attract accusations, and a congregation that acts on the first serious-sounding claim will lose good men and eventually lose the courage to discipline anyone. The next verse is equally blunt about the other danger: them that sin, rebuke before all, that others also may fear.
roots_summary: Greek presbuterion (G4244), the eldership, presbytery; ekklesia (G1577), church, assembly; sunago (G4863), to gather together; marturon (G3144), witnesses.
roots_lines: Greek presbuterion (G4244) — body of elders; 1 Timothy 4:14, Luke 22:66, Acts 22:5.
Greek edoxe to pneumati to hagio kai hemin — it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us; Acts 15:28.
Greek epi duo e trion marturon (G3144) — before two or three witnesses; 1 Timothy 5:19, 2 Corinthians 13:1, Deuteronomy 19:15.
usage: “The apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter”.
“It seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” — the most careful sentence in the chapter.
“Receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses” — receive not.

pos: n. pl. (the princes of the Roman church, ranking next below the pope and electing him)
etymology: Latin cardo, a hinge — the men on whom the government of the church is said to turn. The college took its present form in the eleventh century; the scarlet dates from the thirteenth.
biblical_def: The cardinals form a princely order within the church. Christ forbids the pattern by name: “ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:25–26). He forbids the titles: “be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren… neither be ye called masters” (Mat 23:8–10). He inverts the ranking: “he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Luk 22:26). Peter, whose successors they claim to advise, writes “neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3). And John names the type (3Jn 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cardinal as an ecclesiastical prince in the Romish church, who has a voice in the conclave at the election of a pope; and cardinal as an adjective, chief, principal, preeminent, or fundamental.
webster_full: CARDINAL, a. Chief, principal, preeminent, or fundamental; as the cardinal virtues, which pagans supposed to be justice, prudence, temperance and fortitude.
CARDINAL, n. An ecclesiastical prince in the Romish church, who has a voice in the conclave at the election of a pope, who is taken from their number.
The cardinals are divided into three classes, bishops, priests and deacons.
scriptures: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
corruption_summary: The court of a temporal prince is reproduced inside the church, and every tradition builds one eventually.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 22:26 is the most damning setting for these verses, and it is worth remembering where the dispute occurred. The disciples were arguing about which of them should be accounted the greatest — at the Last Supper, after the bread and the cup, with the betrayal already in motion. The Lord's reply gives the whole doctrine of Christian office in two clauses: he that is greatest, as the younger; he that is chief, as he that doth serve. And then He says, I am among you as he that serveth, which is the only argument He offers.

Matthew 23:8–10 is not a wooden prohibition of every honorific — Paul calls himself a father to the Corinthians in the next breath after refusing to lord it over their faith — but a prohibition of a class of men set above the brotherhood by title. The clause that carries it is all ye are brethren. Whatever offices a church has, they operate inside a brotherhood, and the moment an office puts a man outside it, on a different footing before God, the arrangement has failed regardless of what it is called.

It is easy for a Protestant to read this entry as an attack on somebody else, and dishonest to leave it there. Every tradition grows a court. The celebrity pastor with an entourage and no one able to rebuke him, the conference platform that functions as a hierarchy without a constitution, the denominational office that outranks a congregation in practice while disclaiming it in theory — each is a college of cardinals without the scarlet. The test is not the vestment but the question Matthew 20 puts: is authority here exercised over people, or spent on them?
roots_summary: Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to exercise lordship over; kathegetes (G2519), master, guide; adelphoi (G80), brethren; diakoneo (G1247), to serve.
roots_lines: Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; Matthew 20:25, Mark 10:42, 1 Peter 5:3.
Greek kathegetes (G2519) — master, leader; Matthew 23:10 only.
Greek ho diakonon (G1247) — he that serveth; Luke 22:26–27.
usage: “But it shall not be so among you” — stated as a contrast of systems.
“All ye are brethren” — the clause that carries the prohibition.
“I am among you as he that serveth” — the only argument He offers.

pos: n. (the repeal of a law by authority; the setting aside of the ceremonial ordinances by Christ)
etymology: Latin abrogare, to repeal, from ab-, away, and rogare, to propose a law. A law is abrogated only by the authority that gave it — which is the whole point in this case.
biblical_def: Abrogation is repeal by competent authority. Hebrews says the ceremonial commandment has been repealed: “there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof” (Heb 7:18); “in that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away” (Heb 8:13). Paul says the handwriting of ordinances was cancelled at the cross: “blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… nailing it to his cross” (Col 2:14), and that Christ “abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” (Eph 2:15). But the moral law is not touched: “Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil” (Mat 5:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abrogation as the act of abrogating; a repeal by authority of the legislative power; and abrogate as to repeal, to annul by an authoritative act.
webster_full: ABROGATE, v.t. To repeal; to annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor; applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances.
ABROGATION, n. The act of abrogating; a repeal by authority of the legislative power.
scriptures: Heb 7:18
For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.
Heb 8:13
In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.
Col 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
Eph 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
Mat 5:17
Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
corruption_summary: The whole law is treated as repealed or none of it is, and the confessions distinguish three kinds for exactly this reason.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed division of the Mosaic law into moral, ceremonial and judicial is not an arbitrary convenience; it exists because the New Testament plainly treats different parts differently. The ceremonial is declared fulfilled and repealed — Hebrews devotes chapters to the point, and Peter's sheet full of unclean beasts settles the food laws by direct revelation. The judicial expired with the state it governed, though its general equity remains instructive. The moral law is nowhere repealed; nine of the ten commandments are restated in the epistles as binding, and the Lord's own words in Matthew 5:17 are that He came not to destroy but to fulfil.

Colossians 2:14 gives the most vivid image of what happened and it is legal: the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, blotted out, taken out of the way, nailing it to his cross. The word is the term for a certificate of debt in a man's own hand — an acknowledged obligation, not a disputed one. The cancellation is not a declaration that the debt was never real; it is a receipt, and the receipt was posted where everyone could see it. That is why the following verses forbid anyone to judge a believer in meat or drink or holy days: the account is settled and cannot be reopened by a scruple.

Hebrews 8:13 adds a note of tenderness that is easy to miss. That which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away — written while the temple was still standing and the sacrifices still being offered, within a few years of their ending forever. The old order is not denounced as wicked; it is described as aged, having done its work. What was abrogated was good in its time, given by God, and pointed the whole way to what replaced it, which is why the epistle spends so long showing the correspondence rather than simply announcing the repeal.
roots_summary: Greek athetesis (G115), disannulling, setting aside; palaioo (G3822), to make old; exaleipho (G1813), to blot out, wipe away; katargeo (G2673), to abolish, render inoperative.
roots_lines: Greek athetesis (G115) — disannulling, a setting aside; Hebrews 7:18, 9:26 — both occurrences.
Greek cheirographon (G5498) — handwriting, a bond in one's own hand; Colossians 2:14 only.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to abolish, make of none effect; Ephesians 2:15, 2 Timothy 1:10, Romans 3:31 — where it is denied of the law.
usage: “A disannulling of the commandment going before” — by the authority that gave it.
“Nailing it to his cross” — a receipt, posted publicly.
“I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil” — and the moral law is untouched.

pos: adj. (that cannot be dissolved or loosed; of a bond binding for life)
etymology: Latin indissolubilis, from dissolvere, to loosen apart. Applied chiefly to marriage, and to the union between Christ and His people, which Scripture describes in the same figure.
biblical_def: An indissoluble bond cannot be loosed at will. The Lord grounds marriage in creation and seals it: “they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6). Paul states the duration: “The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth” (1Co 7:39); “the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth” (Rom 7:2). The same figure carries the union with Christ, which is explicitly called a great mystery “concerning Christ and the church” (Eph 5:32). And that union is the one bond named as proof against every power: nothing “shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 8:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indissoluble as not capable of being dissolved or broken; that cannot be broken or rightfully violated; perpetually binding or obligatory, as an indissoluble league or covenant.
webster_full: INDISSOLUBLE, a. That cannot be dissolved; not capable of being liquefied.
2. That cannot be broken or rightfully violated; perpetually binding or obligatory; as an indissoluble league or covenant.
INDISSOLUBLY, adv. In a manner resisting separation; firmly united beyond the power of separation.
scriptures: Mat 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord.
Rom 7:2
For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband.
Eph 5:32
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
Rom 8:39
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
corruption_summary: Marriage is treated as a contract terminable at will, or as a bond so absolute that a spouse must remain in danger.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 19:6 gives the doctrine and its ground in a single movement. The Lord goes behind Moses to the creation — He which made them at the beginning made them male and female — and then declares what God has done: God hath joined together. The bond is not merely a promise the parties made and may therefore unmake; it is an act of God upon them, which is why the prohibition is addressed to third parties as much as to the couple. Let not man put asunder covers the friend, the relative and the culture that makes dissolution easy.

The Reformed have never taught that indissolubility is absolute in a fallen world, and honesty about the exceptions is part of holding the doctrine well. The Lord Himself names one in the same passage; Paul names another in 1 Corinthians 7 when an unbelieving spouse departs; and the confessions have historically applied these with care rather than treating every marriage as beyond remedy whatever occurs. A doctrine of indissolubility that requires a wife to remain in the house of a man who is destroying her has stopped protecting what it was given to protect, and has become the instrument of the very hardness of heart Christ was rebuking.

Ephesians 5:32 explains why the stakes are as high as they are. Marriage is a figure of something — this is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church — and the permanence is part of what it signifies. Christ does not leave, and the love that will not be separated from us in Romans 8 is set out in a list that includes death, life, angels, principalities, things present and things to come. A marriage that holds through what would ordinarily end it is preaching something true about Him, and this is the strongest argument for the covenant that exists: not that leaving is forbidden, but that staying tells the truth.
roots_summary: Greek suzeugnumi (G4801), to yoke together; chorizo (G5563), to separate, put asunder; deo (G1210), to bind; musterion (G3466), mystery.
roots_lines: Greek sunezeuxen (G4801) — hath joined together, yoked; Matthew 19:6, Mark 10:9 — both occurrences.
Greek chorizo (G5563) — to separate; Matthew 19:6, 1 Corinthians 7:10–15, Romans 8:35, 8:39.
Greek dedetai (G1210) — is bound; 1 Corinthians 7:39, Romans 7:2.
usage: “What therefore God hath joined together” — an act of God, not only a promise.
“Let not man put asunder” — addressed to third parties too.
“This is a great mystery… concerning Christ and the church” — why the stakes are high.
